Take with water; with food if GI upset
Reduce dose / avoid in significant impairment
CBC, LFTs and renal function if prolonged; CNS effects
summary: Nalidixic acid is a first-generation quinolone antibacterial active mainly against Gram-negative urinary pathogens, used to treat and suppress urinary tract infections. It is NO LONGER marketed in the United States (withdrawn) and is little used elsewhere, having been superseded by fluoroquinolones. The usual adult dose is 1 g four times daily for 1-2 weeks, reduced to 500 mg four times daily for long-term suppression. Notable risks include CNS effects (seizures, raised intracranial pressure), photosensitivity, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency and possible cartilage toxicity.
indications: Treatment of urinary tract infections caused by susceptible Gram-negative organisms (E. coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter)
Long-term suppression of recurrent urinary tract infection (reduced dose)

dosage.d: 1 g four times daily for 1-2 weeks
~50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses (acute); 30 mg/kg/day for suppression

admin: Take orally with a full glass of water; with food if it causes stomach upset
Avoid excessive sun/UV exposure because of photosensitivity
moa: Nalidixic acid inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (DNA topoisomerase II), blocking the supercoiling and replication of bacterial DNA. This is bactericidal against susceptible Gram-negative bacilli; its activity is concentrated in the urinary tract, where it achieves adequate antibacterial levels.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to nalidixic acid or other quinolones
relative: Cerebral arteriosclerosis or conditions lowering seizure threshold
monitor: CBC, liver and renal function on prolonged therapy
Signs of hemolysis in at-risk patients

preg: Avoid in pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester and near term, because of the risk of hemolysis and potential effects on fetal cartilage; use only if no safer alternative exists.
lact: Avoid breastfeeding while taking nalidixic acid; it is excreted into breast milk and has caused hemolytic anemia in G6PD-deficient infants.
renal: Excreted renally; reduce the dose and use with caution in significant renal impairment, and avoid in severe impairment where urinary concentrations may be inadequate and systemic accumulation occurs.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; cholestatic jaundice has been reported. Avoid in significant hepatic disease.

major: Warfarin - nalidixic acid potentiates anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
Other quinolones - cross-reactivity and additive CNS/photosensitivity risk
moderate: Antacids, sucralfate, iron and divalent cations - chelate and reduce absorption
Probenecid - reduces urinary excretion, lowering efficacy
minor: Melphalan - reported severe enterocolitis when combined
interactions.food: May take with food if GI upset; separate from antacids/iron by at least 2 hours.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause false-positive urine glucose with copper-reduction (Benedict's/Clinitest) tests; may raise LFTs.

serious: Seizures and raised intracranial pressure (especially in children/infants)
Severe cutaneous reactions and photosensitivity reactions

monitoring: Complete blood count, liver and renal function if treatment exceeds 2 weeks
CNS symptoms - headache, visual disturbance, drowsiness, seizures
Signs of hemolysis in susceptible patients
counsel: Take with plenty of water and finish the whole course
Protect your skin from strong sunlight; you may sunburn more easily
Separate antacids, iron or dairy from your dose by a couple of hours
Report severe headache, visual changes, drowsiness or a fit
Avoid driving if you feel dizzy or drowsy
pk: Antibacterial urinary levels within hours of dosing
Plasma peak about 1-2 hours after an oral dose
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: NO LONGER marketed in the USA (withdrawn) and largely obsolete - information is based on historical FDA labeling, BNF and SmPC sources
Confined to urinary tract infection; achieves antibacterial levels only in urine, not in blood/tissue
Contraindicated in epilepsy, G6PD deficiency, porphyria and infants under 3 months
Causes false-positive urine glucose with copper-reduction tests
Resistance emerges quickly; superseded by fluoroquinolones
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, then skip it - do not double up. Keeping the four-times-daily schedule maintains effective urinary antibacterial levels.
overdose: Overdose can cause toxic psychosis, convulsions, raised intracranial pressure, metabolic acidosis, vomiting and visual disturbance. There is no specific antidote - manage with airway protection, anticonvulsants for seizures, correction of acidosis, generous fluids and supportive care; the drug is highly protein bound so dialysis is of limited value.
